verified.title: R7 'retraining flow when new data arrives' marked VERIFIED, but no trigger exists in the package
verified.issue: R7 status reads 'VERIFIED: ... drift/new-data trigger + gated promotion'. The PDF's MLOps layer asks to 'show a simple retraining flow when new data arrives'. Nothing in src/sentinelloop watches for new data or starts a retrain on a drift alarm; the only retraining lives in an experiment script that runs its scenarios unconditionally.
verified.evidence: src/sentinelloop/retrain.py is 35 lines containing only evaluate_gate(); grep -rniE 'new data|trigger|retrain' src/sentinelloop/*.py returns no trigger code (only policy.trigger_series and dashboard reads). experiments/e4_retrain_gate.py lines 92-106 call scenario('A_accept_more_data') and scenario('B_reject_corrupted_data') unconditionally; the drift check (lines 108-135) is computed afterwards and gates nothing. pipeline.py line 180 uses drift_report.alarm only as an agent escalation input. The slide box 'RETRAIN JOB triggered by a drift alarm or a new data file' (make_round1_slide.py:85) therefore describes design intent, not code.
verified.recommendation: Either add a minimal `python -m sentinelloop retrain --subset X` that runs when a file appears under data/incoming/ or when the stored drift report has alarm=true, and log it, or downgrade R7 to PARTIALLY VERIFIED ('gate and promotion verified; trigger is a scripted experiment') and reword the slide box to 'retrain job (gated); trigger: drift alarm or new file (design)'.

verdicts.reasoning: Every factual claim in the finding reproduces. docs/OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md line 56 reads exactly 'R7 | Retraining flow when new data arrives | drift/new-data trigger + gated promotion | VERIFIED: E4 drift trigger 4/4 subsets; ...' and, unlike every other VERIFIED row, names no source file. src/sentinelloop/retrain.py is 35 lines: a GateResult dataclass and evaluate_gate(); nothing watches a directory or reacts to an alarm. The cited grep over src/sentinelloop/*.py returns only policy.trigger_series (an agent-policy function), dashboard/viewdata reads of retrain_log.json, and a docstring in models.py. experiments/e4_retrain_gate.py calls scenario('A_accept_more_data') at line 92 and scenario('B_reject_corrupted_data') at line 100 unconditionally; the drift monitor is fitted and checked only afterwards (lines 108-135) and its result is written to the log as a 'C_drift_trigger' summary row (decision=None in all four artifacts/FD00x/retrain_log.json) that gates nothing. pipeline.py uses drift_report.alarm only as an agent observation input (lines 180, 216) and a metric (143); it never starts a retrain. data/incoming/ does not exist, and cli.py exposes only doctor/data/baseline/run/audit/dashboard (no 'retrain' subcommand, although docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md line 65 lists one). The Round 1 slide box at submission/make_round1_slide.py:85 ('RETRAIN JOB triggered by a drift alarm or a new data file') therefore describes intent. Severity is lowered from high to medium because: (a) the PDF asks for a 'simple retraining flow when new data arrives' and Round 2 asks for 'a demo retraining run', and E4 does train a challenger on champion+new engines, gate it, version it in MLflow and log the outcome, so the substance is demonstrated; (b) SYSTEM_DESIGN.md is explicitly headed 'Status: PROPOSED (design)' and INNOVATION_HYPOTHESES.md line 19 already calls E4 'scripted accept / reject / drift-trigger scenarios', so the scripted nature is partially disclosed; (c) the only judged deliverable so far is the Round 1 design slide, where a 'triggered by' box is acceptable design language. What remains is a genuine overclaim in the project's own compliance table ('VERIFIED' for a trigger that has no code) that would be exposed in a Round 2 code probe and is cheap to fix by downgrading R7 to PARTIALLY VERIFIED or adding a minimal trigger command.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is literally true and is NOT disclosed anywhere, so it stands; but 'high' is inflated. What the rubric actually asks: the PDF's MLOps layer wants a 'simple retraining flow when new data arrives' and Round 2 wants 'a demo retraining run'. E4 scenario A is exactly that flow (30% new engines arrive -> challenger trained on champion+new -> three gates -> PROMOTE/REJECT, logged to MLflow with champion alias moved and to artifacts/<subset>/retrain_log.json, which the dashboard shows). A scripted demo satisfies 'demo retraining run'; no student-competition judge expects a file watcher or cron. MLOps in action is 10% of Round 2 and the trigger is one element of it; Round 1 is a design deck where 'triggered by a drift alarm or a new data file' is acceptable as intent. So competition impact is bounded. Why it is not low: (1) the project's stated honesty rule is 'nothing is hidden in the deck', and R7 is marked VERIFIED for a trigger that has no code; (2) the overclaim is wider than the finding says: docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md line 61 states retrain.py contains 'Trigger (new data file in data/incoming/ or drift alarm)' (data/incoming/ does not exist) and line 65 lists CLI subcommands 'train, evaluate, replay, stress, retrain, stream' that do not exist (actual: doctor, data, baseline, run, audit, dashboard). SYSTEM_DESIGN.md is a submission artefact (cited for R12 'documented design'), so a judge who reads it and runs `python -m sentinelloop --help` sees six phantom commands in seconds, which is a credibility hit for a project whose differentiation (D11) is honesty and traceability; (3) 'drift trigger fully supported' in EXPERIMENT_RESULTS E4 means the monitor alarms correctly on shifted/biased windows with 0/20 false alarms, i.e. a detection test, so a reader could reasonably believe alarm->retrain linkage exists. Recommendation adds value and is cheap: downgrade R7 to PARTIALLY VERIFIED, fix the SYSTEM_DESIGN retrain.py and cli.py rows, and either add a thin wrapper or label the slide/design-doc trigger as design. Corrected severity: medium.

verified.title: SYSTEM_DESIGN.md documents CLI commands, a retrain trigger, DB tables and artefacts that do not exist, while PROJECT_STATUS says it is aligned
verified.issue: The PDF ground rule is 'document the design clearly so it can be explained in a review'. The final design doc lists `cli.py` commands 'doctor, data, train, evaluate, replay, stress, retrain, stream, dashboard, run' (line 65), a retrain.py 'Trigger (new data file in data/incoming/ or drift alarm)' (line 61), SQLite tables 'retrain_log, drift_log' (line 70) and artefacts 'model_quantile.pkl', 'predictions_oof_train.csv' (line 68). PROJECT_STATUS.md line 54 states 'docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md ... aligned with the built components'.
verified.evidence: src/sentinelloop/cli.py lines 85-92 register only doctor, data, baseline, run, audit, dashboard. Read-only sqlite query of artifacts/sentinelloop.db: tables = ['decisions', 'work_orders', 'runs']. ls artifacts/FD001 shows model_cqr.pkl and no predictions_oof_train.csv. No data/incoming handling anywhere in src/.
verified.recommendation: Rewrite rows 61, 65, 68, 70 of SYSTEM_DESIGN.md to the built interface (six CLI commands, three tables, model_cqr.pkl, OOF predictions under experiments/results/oof) and remove the 'aligned' claim from PROJECT_STATUS until a doc-vs-code check has been run.

verdicts.reasoning: Every factual claim in the finding reproduces exactly. docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md line 65 lists ten CLI commands (doctor, data, train, evaluate, replay, stress, retrain, stream, dashboard, run); src/sentinelloop/cli.py build_parser() lines 85-92 registers only doctor, data, baseline, run, audit, dashboard, and src/sentinelloop/__main__.py routes `python -m sentinelloop` to that parser, so `train`, `evaluate`, `replay`, `stress`, `retrain`, `stream` would all fail with an argparse error. Line 95 of the same doc additionally advertises `python -m sentinelloop stream --subset FD001 --units 5`, which does not exist. Line 61 describes a retrain trigger on `data/incoming/`; retrain.py defines only `GateResult` and `evaluate_gate`, there is no data/incoming directory (data/ contains only raw/) and no reference to 'incoming' anywhere in src/. Line 70 lists SQLite tables retrain_log and drift_log; a read-only sqlite query of artifacts/sentinelloop.db returns exactly ['decisions', 'runs', 'work_orders'] (the doc also omits the real `runs` table). Line 68 lists model_quantile.pkl and predictions_oof_train.csv; artifacts/FD001 contains model_cqr.pkl (matching pipeline.py line 246) and no OOF file, with OOF outputs living under experiments/results/oof/FD00x_full.csv. PROJECT_STATUS.md line 54 affirmatively states SYSTEM_DESIGN.md was 'aligned with the built components' in Phase 5, which is false, and no other doc (KNOWN_LIMITATIONS, DECISION_LOG, REPRODUCIBILITY, README, submission/) discloses the gap. Severity lowered from high to medium because the judge-facing path is not broken: README.md lines 34-37, DEMO_RUNBOOK.md, DEMO_SCRIPT.md, CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md and REPRODUCIBILITY.md all cite only the six real commands, SYSTEM_DESIGN.md line 3 self-labels as 'PROPOSED (design)', and no result or claimed metric depends on the stale rows. It remains a genuine 'document the design clearly' compliance defect compounded by a false alignment statement, which a reviewer who opens the design doc would notice and penalise, and the fix is a few table rows.

PROJECT_STATUS line 54 claims SYSTEM_DESIGN.md is 'aligned with the built components' and OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS R12 marks 'documented design' VERIFIED citing this file, so the project's own verification vocabulary is wrong here. KNOWN_LIMITATIONS (23 items), FAILURE_ANALYSIS and EXPERIMENT_RESULTS contain no mention of design-doc drift, so the default-refute condition does not apply and the recommendation (rewrite rows 61/65/68/70, drop the 'aligned' claim) is concrete and not redundant. Severity is inflated from high, though: SYSTEM_DESIGN.md line 3 labels itself 'Status: PROPOSED (design)'; every module in its component table (stress.py, replay.py, stream.py, retrain.py, policy.py) exists and the capabilities are reachable via `run --stream-units` and experiments/e3,e4,e5 scripts, so this is an interface/naming mismatch, not a missing capability; the judge-facing surfaces (README.md command table, REPRODUCIBILITY.md stage commands, submission/round2_deck_content.md `python -m sentinelloop run --subset all`) are all correct; and nothing in README or submission/ links to SYSTEM_DESIGN.md, so a judge reaches it only by browsing docs/. No scored result or slide claim changes. It stays medium rather than low because the ground rule R12 is evidenced by this exact file, the doc hands a reviewer a demo command that fails, the retrain row implies a data/incoming trigger that was never built, and two status documents assert a verification that was not performed, which is the kind of self-inflicted credibility hit a rigour-focused entry cannot afford. Cheap, mechanical fix.

verified.title: Scripted demo retraining run is on FD001, whose stored retrain log contains only REJECT decisions (no PROMOTE row to show)
verified.issue: Round 2 requires 'a demo retraining run'. The runbook produces artefacts with `run --subset FD001` (line 16) and tells the presenter to show 'retraining log with the PROMOTE and REJECT rows' (line 36). On FD001 the expected-PROMOTE scenario was rejected in both E4 runs, so the dashboard will show rows with as_expected:false and no accept path. The Round 1 slide also states 'accept AND reject paths are demonstrated' (make_round1_slide.py:92) without saying on which subsets.
verified.evidence: artifacts/FD001/retrain_log.json: decisions = A_accept_more_data REJECT ('picp 0.800 < 0.85'), B REJECT, secondary A REJECT ('picp 0.835 < 0.85'), B REJECT, B2 REJECT. experiments/results/e4_retrain_gate/summary.json and e4_retrain_gate_secondary/summary.json: PROMOTE on A occurs only for FD002 and FD003 (both runs) and FD004 (primary only). Python listing of all four retrain logs confirms FD001 has zero PROMOTE rows.
verified.recommendation: Run the demo on FD003 (PROMOTE and REJECT with reasons in both runs, 100 test engines, RMSE 13.88) or show the FD003 log explicitly; add the subset name next to 'accept AND reject paths are demonstrated' on the slide and in the deck.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding reproduces literally. docs/DEMO_RUNBOOK.md line 16 runs `run --subset FD001 --stream-units 5` and line 36 tells the presenter to show the "retraining log with the PROMOTE and REJECT rows"; line 40 additionally promises MLflow will show an "accepted challenger" for FD001. Loading artifacts/FD001/retrain_log.json gives five gate rows, all REJECT: A_accept_more_data REJECT (picp 0.800 < 0.85, as_expected false), B REJECT, secondary A REJECT (picp 0.835 < 0.85, as_expected false), B REJECT, B2 REJECT. FD002 and FD003 have PROMOTE on A in both runs; FD004 only in the primary. The dashboard (src/sentinelloop/dashboard.py:44, 108-110) renders artifacts/<sidebar subset>/retrain_log.json, the subset list is sorted directories containing metrics.json (viewdata.py:28-32), so FD001 is the default and, if the runbook's step 1 is followed literally, FD002/FD003 never appear in the selector because metrics.json is only written by the pipeline (pipeline.py:237). submission/make_round1_slide.py:92 does say "accept AND reject paths are demonstrated" with no subset. Two further wrinkles: the MLflow "accepted challenger" the runbook promises for FD001 exists in artifacts/mlflow.db only as stale fast-mode smoke runs (champion 16.944, PROMOTE on A; see experiments/results/smoke_fast_fd001*.log), not from the 2026-10-18 full run, and the reset procedure (line 24-25) deletes artifacts/ including mlflow.db and re-runs only the FD001 pipeline, after which there is no retrain_log.json at all until step 1 is repeated. Severity is lowered from high to medium because this is a runbook/staging inconsistency rather than a missing capability: both gate outcomes genuinely exist in stored artefacts, the Round 2 deck plan (submission/round2_deck_content.md slide 9) already names FD002/FD003 for the promoted challenger, DEMO_SCRIPT.md Beat 5 already scripts the caveat that the 0.85 floor rejected two better-RMSE challengers, and the FD001 false rejection is disclosed in EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md (lines 58, 64, 70) and KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md item 21. The optional FD004 run on runbook line 17 would also put a PROMOTE row on screen. The fix is a one-line change (demo on FD003 or FD004, or select that subset in the sidebar, and name the subset on the slide), but as written a presenter following the runbook will show a log with only REJECT rows, two of them flagged as_expected:false, directly under a slide claim of a demonstrated accept path, which a judge scoring Demo & explanation or MLOps in action could penalise.

verdicts.reasoning: The factual core is correct (artifacts/FD001/retrain_log.json has 0 PROMOTE and 5 REJECT rows; DEMO_RUNBOOK.md:36 says "PROMOTE and REJECT rows"), but the finding mis-scopes what the scripted demo shows, ignores that the fact is disclosed in every judged artefact, and its recommendation adds nothing a judge would reward. (1) The scripted demo already shows the accept path: runbook step 3 line 37 sends the presenter to the Experiments tab, which renders e4_retrain_gate and e4_retrain_gate_secondary tables for all four subsets (dashboard.py:112-121 reads every experiments/results/<exp>/summary.json independently of the sidebar subset), including PROMOTE on FD002/FD003 in both runs; step 5 opens the MLflow `sentinelloop-retrain` experiment, which holds 13 runs tagged gate=PROMOTE across subsets. The dashboard also has a sidebar Subset selectbox (dashboard.py:44, viewdata.py:60 loads retrain_log per subset), and the runbook's optional FD004 run (line 17) yields a log with 3 PROMOTE / 2 REJECT rows. E4 via `run_all.py --skip-pipeline` needs only raw data (common.prepared), so all four retrain logs exist on the demo laptop. (2) The FD001 rejection is disclosed everywhere a judge looks: EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md lines 58 and 70 (FD001 REJECT with picp reasons in both runs), FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md item 8, KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md item 21, DECISION_LOG D21, CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C13 ("more-data challenger promoted on FD002–FD004; corrupted challenger rejected on FD001 only") and C14, and DEMO_SCRIPT.md beat 5 narrates it out loud as a caveat. (3) The finding's claim that the deck does not say which subsets is wrong: round2_deck_content.md slide 9 states "more-data challenger promoted on FD002/FD003; label-corrupted challenger rejected on all four subsets". The Round 1 slide caption "accept AND reject paths are demonstrated" is true at project level and Round 1 is not judged on MLOps-in-action. (4) Official requirement (OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md:38) is "a demo retraining run"; a run that rejects a challenger with a logged reason satisfies it, and the team's own script treats the FD001 rejection as evidence of honesty. What remains is a one-phrase inaccuracy in an internal presenter note (runbook line 36 could read "REJECT rows on FD001; PROMOTE rows via the Experiments tab or sidebar subset FD004"). Switching the whole demo to FD003, as recommended, would break the runbook's FD001-specific expected console numbers, timings and registry name for no judged benefit. Not high; at most a low-severity wording nit.

The Unstop listing (quoted in OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md line 15) requires 2-3 members from the same college; a slide with a placeholder reads as unfinished and may fail an identity check.
verified.evidence: round1_slide.png top-right text: 'Team SentinelLoop · (college to be filled)'. make_round1_slide.py line 51 default `--team 'Team ______  ·  ______ College'`. OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md line 63 R14: 'PARTIALLY VERIFIED: ... team/college placeholder'.
verified.recommendation: Re-render with `--team` set to the real names before upload and make the script refuse to write the PDF when the team string contains '___' or 'to be filled'.

verdicts.reasoning: The observation reproduces literally: both submission/round1_slide.png and submission/round1_slide.pdf (same savefig call, same 03:46 mtime) carry 'Team SentinelLoop · (college to be filled)' in the title band, and the script default (line 51) and Makefile TEAM variable are both underscore placeholders. But the finding fails the 'already disclosed' test on its own evidence: docs/OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md R14 (line 63) already marks the slide PARTIALLY VERIFIED for exactly 'team/college placeholder', and submission/CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md C22 lists the regenerate command as `make_round1_slide.py --team "..."`. The college name is information only the humans hold; the pipeline cannot fill it, and the project explicitly leaves it as a flag to be set at render time. The Round 1 window closes 24 Oct 2026 (today is 18 Oct); nothing has been uploaded, so 'the file that would be uploaded' is the reviewer's assumption, not a fact. The 'may fail an identity check' claim is unsupported: nothing in the project or the quoted Unstop text says the slide is the identity source (registration collects member/college details), and the reviewer offers no evidence for it. A judge only sees this if the team uploads the checked-in draft without the one-flag re-render the project already documents. Rated 'high' as a compliance defect it is refuted; what remains is a low-priority hardening the project has not yet done: there is no guard in make_round1_slide.py against writing a PDF whose --team string contains '___' or 'to be filled', and the pre-submit items in PROJECT_STATUS.md line 17 and SCORING_AND_RISKS.md K1 do not explicitly list 'set --team to the real names before upload'. Adding that guard and checklist line is worth five minutes before 24 Oct, but it is a known TODO, not a hidden compliance failure.

verified.title: FD004 raw RMSE quoted as 27.1 in two submission documents; the artefact and the rendered slide say 27.0
verified.issue: C1 and round1_slide_content.md line 37 state 'FD004 15.4 / 27.1'. The artefact value is 27.0486, which the slide script prints as 27.0. The matrix's own promise is that every number is copied from an artefact, so the two documents disagree with the artefact and with the slide a judge will see.
verified.evidence: artifacts/FD004/metrics.json hgbr_rmse_raw = 27.048590629322145; experiments/results/e0_baseline/FD004_metrics.json identical. round1_slide.png bottom-left: 'FD004 15.4 / 27.0'. verified.recommendation: Change both documents to 27.0 (or print two decimals everywhere) and add a one-line script that diffs every number in the matrix against the JSON it cites.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is literally true as stated: both artefacts hold hgbr_rmse_raw = 27.048590629322145 for FD004; the slide script (make_round1_slide.py line 119) formats it with `:.1f`, which I reproduced as "FD004 15.4 / 27.0", and the rendered round1_slide.png bottom-left panel visibly reads "FD004 15.4 / 27.0". CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md line 7 says "FD004 15.4/27.1" and round1_slide_content.md line 37 says "FD004 15.4 / 27.1". README.md line 14, round2_deck_content.md line 11, docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md and docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md all say 27.05, which is correct at two decimals. So two supporting documents disagree by 0.05 with the artefact and with the rendered slide, and the matrix's own "every number from an artefact" promise is technically broken for C1. However, "high" overstates it: the discrepancy is a classic double-rounding of 27.05 to 27.1 (half-up), it does not alter any claim, ranking or conclusion, the deliverable a Round 1 judge actually sees (the PDF/PNG) is correct, and the Round 2 deck content is correct. A judge cross-checking the matrix could notice the inconsistency and it mildly undercuts the project's auditability pitch, so it is worth the one-character fix, but it would not materially cost points. Severity corrected to low. Note FD002's 27.1 is correct (raw 27.1018), so only FD004 needs changing.

verified.title: Anomaly detection (half of the PDF's ML layer) has no reported performance on real degradation and never produces a work order
verified.issue: R4 'Detect abnormal behaviour' is marked VERIFIED on the strength of a unit test and a WATCH rule. No metric is reported for detection of actual degradation (lead time before failure, false-positive rate in healthy life on out-of-fold engines); the only anomaly numbers in the artefacts are flag rates without ground truth. The entry's own results document admits the anomaly input changes nothing in the policy metrics, and the agent code shows WATCH can never open an order.
verified.evidence: artifacts/<subset>/metrics.json contains only anomaly_flag_rate_test_last_cycle (0.16 / 0.19 / 0.22 / 0.08) and anomaly_threshold. tests/test_anomaly.py lines 15-24 assert only that late-life flags exceed early-life flags and early-life rate <= 0.10. docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md line 93: 'ablation (iii) "anomaly input to the agent" was not run; by construction the anomaly input only sets WATCH severities and the conflicting-evidence escalation reason, neither of which enters the E1 policy metrics'. src/sentinelloop/agent.py line 88-89 (WATCH only when lower > t_medium) and line 15 ORDER_SEVERITIES = ('HIGH', 'CRITICAL'). E3 measures injected faults, not degradation.
verified.recommendation: Add an out-of-fold evaluation on complete training engines: cycles between first sustained flag and failure (lead time), fraction of engines flagged before failure, false-alarm rate in the first 40% of life; report it in metrics.json and on deck slide 5, and state plainly that the health index informs WATCH/escalation only.

verdicts.reasoning: Every cited fact reproduces. docs/OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS.md line 53 marks R4 VERIFIED on 'tests/test_anomaly.py; sustained-anomaly WATCH rule in the agent' and nothing else. tests/test_anomaly.py lines 15-24 run on make_synthetic_raw (not C-MAPSS) and assert only late-life flag rate > early-life rate and early rate <= 0.10. All four artifacts/<subset>/metrics.json carry exactly two anomaly keys, anomaly_threshold and anomaly_flag_rate_test_last_cycle (0.16 / 0.189 / 0.22 / 0.085), with no ground truth. docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md line 93 contains the quoted sentence verbatim (ablation (iii) not run; anomaly only sets WATCH and the conflicting-evidence reason). src/sentinelloop/agent.py line 15 ORDER_SEVERITIES = ('HIGH','CRITICAL') and line 119 wants_order = escalate or severity in ORDER_SEVERITIES, so WATCH alone never opens an order; tests/test_agent.py line 82-85 asserts exactly that. E3 (experiments/e3_stress.py, docs line 40-51) corrupts the last 20 cycles with injected faults and measures change-relative detection; it is not a degradation-detection metric. No lead-time / flagged-before-failure / healthy-life false-alarm number exists in any results README, CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md, the deck plan (slide 5 lists only RMSE/PHM08/PICP/MPIW) or KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md (item 7 only says the index 'does not identify fault modes'). The disclosure on results line 93 is buried in the E7 ablation paragraph and is not carried to the deck or the requirements table. Two corrections lower the severity from high to medium: (1) the title's 'never produces a work order' is slightly overstated, since anomaly_flag with rul_lower > 100 fires R_ESC_CONFLICT and opens an INSPECTION order (agent.py line 99), though in the full run this fired only 7 of 3,409 decisions (FD003 6, FD004 1) and WATCH fired 1/1/83/1 times, so the layer is nearly inert in practice; (2) the raw material for the recommended metric already exists: experiments/results/oof/<subset>_full_bl.csv carries out-of-fold anomaly_flag and failure_cycle for every complete training engine, and a one-liner over it gives engines flagged before failure 100% / 91% / 60% / 64% (FD001-FD004), median lead 18 / 27 / 56.5 / 21 cycles, engine-level false alarms in the first 40% of life 0 / 1.2 / 8 / 2.8%. So the detector does work on real degradation and the fix is minutes of work, but the unreported numbers also expose a genuine weakness (36-40% of FD003/FD004 engines never raise a sustained flag before failure) that the entry currently neither knows nor states. A judge scoring 'Model performance' or 'ML approach' against the PDF's 'detect abnormal behaviour and predict RUL' would find half the ML layer with no evaluated number, so this is a real, undisclosed gap, but a reporting gap on a secondary component rather than a broken one.

verified.title: Stored E3 output shows a severe false drift alarm on untouched FD003 test engines; docs claim 0 false alarms and attribute every fleet alarm to the fault
verified.issue: The age-matched drift monitor fires 'severe_single_feature' on the early-life rows of the 50 CLEAN (uncorrupted) FD003 test engines in all five fault scenarios. EXPERIMENT_RESULTS reports 'fleet drift alarm: yes (all)' as fault detection and E4 reports '0 false alarms in 20 clean windows on every subset', never mentioning this column.
verified.evidence: All five FD003 rows in e3_stress/summary.json have 'fleet_drift_alarm_clean_early': True (FD001/FD002/FD004 rows: False). Reproduced read-only from artifacts/FD003/drift_monitor.pkl with the E3 seed-42 split: 50 clean engines -> alarm True, reasons ['severe_single_feature'], s9_rm PSI 1.53; all 100 test engines -> alarm False, s9_rm PSI 0.27; the other 50 engines uncorrupted -> alarm False. docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:45-49 column 'fleet drift alarm' = 'yes (all)'; :65 '0 false alarms in 20 age-matched clean windows on every subset'. src/sentinelloop/drift.py:106 severe rule 'v > self.severe_psi_threshold'. E4's 20 'clean windows' are 500-row random samples from one pooled early-life frame (e4_retrain_gate.py:117-122), which averages out engine heterogeneity and so cannot see this failure.
verified.recommendation: Report the fleet_drift_alarm_clean_early column and treat FD003 as a false-alarm case; measure false-alarm rate over many random engine subsets of realistic fleet size rather than overlapping row windows; reconsider or raise the single-feature PSI>1 rule for small fleets.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is literally true and reproduces to the stated numbers. (1) experiments/results/e3_stress/summary.json: all five FD003 rows have "fleet_drift_alarm_clean_early": true (lines 238, 260, 282, 304, 326); every FD001/FD002/FD004 row has false. (2) e3_stress.py:115 computes that column as mon.check on the early-life rows of the 50 uncorrupted engines, i.e. a pure false alarm by construction. (3) Re-running only the inference path on the stored FD003 artefacts (drift_monitor.pkl, seed-42 split from e3_stress.run_subset) gives: 50 clean engines early rows -> alarm True, reasons ['severe_single_feature'], s9_rm PSI 1.525 (finding: 1.53); all 100 engines -> alarm False, s9_rm PSI 0.273 (finding: 0.27); the other 50 engines, uncorrupted -> alarm False. The severe rule is drift.py:106 (v > severe_psi_threshold=1.0, config severe_psi_threshold: 1.0). (4) It is not a one-off split: over 200 random 50-engine subsets of the clean FD003 test fleet the monitor alarms in 21/200 (10.5%), and over 200 random 25-engine subsets in 150/200 (75%). (5) e4_retrain_gate.py:117-122 confirms the E4 "20 clean windows" are 500-row random samples from one pooled early-life frame, which cannot expose per-engine heterogeneity; E4's "0/20" is therefore a weaker test than the column E3 already had. (6) Disclosure: the raw column appears only in the wide results table (e3_stress/README.md, e3_table.csv). docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:45-49 reports the fleet alarm as "yes (all)", :51 says "The fleet-level drift monitor fired on every fault scenario ... so a fleet-wide sensor bias is caught even when individual engines are not", :65 claims "0 false alarms in 20 age-matched clean windows on every subset"; INNOVATION_HYPOTHESES.md:18 ("caught at fleet level (E3)") and DEMO_SCRIPT.md:21 repeat the fleet-level claim as the mitigation for the 4-20% bias detection floor; KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md and FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md do not mention it. A judge would penalise a stated "fleet-level catch" whose monitor also fires on an untouched 50-engine fleet. Corroborating (beyond the finding's literal scope but bearing on the attribution claim): the "mixed_tail" fleet alarm that the docs column reports also fires on the fully CLEAN run on all four subsets (FD001 severe s7_rm PSI 1.86; FD002 severe s6_rm 1.13; FD003 severe s10_slope 1.71; FD004 feature_share), because the trailing window of all engines (end-of-life rows) is compared against an age-matched early-life reference; E3 has no clean-run baseline for that alarm, and agent.py:97-98 escalates any HIGH/CRITICAL decision when drift_flag is set, so part of the full agent's escalations in E3 come from an alarm that is on regardless of the fault. Severity stays high rather than critical because the per-engine H3 metrics (detection, false-alarm, silent-wrong-order) are computed without the drift signal (newly() only counts data_quality/conflicting_evidence), so the 3/4 verdict itself survives; what fails is the fleet-level claim used to excuse the bias failure and the E4 drift-trigger "0 false alarms" claim.

What stands: (1) experiments/results/e3_stress/summary.json carries fleet_drift_alarm_clean_early=True on all five FD003 rows and False on the other 15; the clean half is the same seed-42 split in every fault, so this is one false alarm on one fixed 50-engine subset, repeated five times, not five failures. (2) It is not disclosed anywhere: the string clean_early occurs only in e3_stress.py and the auto-generated results README table; docs/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md, docs/FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md, docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md and docs/DECISION_LOG.md never mention a fleet-level false alarm after the D17 age-matching fix, and FAILURE_ANALYSIS row 9 presents that fix as resolving the whole-population false alarms. The "nothing hidden" ethos the entry sells (README, DEMO_SCRIPT, KNOWN_LIMITATIONS header) makes an omitted contradicting column a credibility risk if an ML reviewer opens the results table, where the True values are visible in plain text. (3) EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:51 ("fleet-level drift monitor fired on every fault scenario ... so a fleet-wide sensor bias is caught even when individual engines are not") is unsupported by E3 for FD003, the very subset where per-engine bias detection is 4-6%: the monitor also fires on FD003's uncorrupted half, so "yes" in that column is not evidence of detection. Worse for that sentence, the "yes (all)" column comes from fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail, which checks the trailing window of all engines against the early-life reference with no clean baseline computed at all (e3_stress.py:111-114), so the E3 fleet column is weak evidence on every subset and clean_early was the only negative control. (4) The fleet alarm is load-bearing: decide(..., drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm) feeds agent rule R_ESC_DRIFT (agent.py:97), which escalates every HIGH/CRITICAL decision when the flag is on, so silent_wrong_order_full=0 is mechanically guaranteed whenever the fleet alarm fires; fleet-alarm false positives therefore matter to the headline, not just to a side column. (5) 50 engines giving s9_rm PSI 1.53 while 100 engines give 0.27 (artifacts/FD003/drift_reference.json confirms 0.273, no alarm) shows the severe single-feature PSI>1 rule is brittle at realistic fleet sizes, and no limitation entry covers PSI sensitivity to fleet size or engine heterogeneity. Why not high: the H3 pre-registered criteria (per-engine detection, per-engine false-alarm rate, silent-wrong-order reduction) do not read the clean_early column and remain correct as stated; the doc's "zero false alarms" in E3 is explicitly the per-engine column and is true; the production FD003 run on all 100 official test engines does not alarm; E4's drift-trigger test independently shows 0/20 clean windows and bias/regime alarms on FD003 (its 500-row pooled sampling is weaker than engine-subset sampling, as the reviewer notes, but it is a separate, truthfully reported result). A competition judge scoring "drift trigger" (15%+10% rubric rows in SCORING_AND_RISKS.md) would be unlikely to find this unaided; an ML reviewer would, and would also catch the overclaiming sentence at line 51. The recommendation (report the column, note FD003 as a fleet-level false-alarm case, measure fleet false-alarm rate over random engine subsets, revisit the PSI>1 rule for small fleets) adds something no document currently says, so it is not refutable as already disclosed.

verified.title: Headline 'escalates only untrustworthy cases to a human' is contradicted by E2 on clean data
verified.issue: The slide title band (also README.md:3 and round2_deck_content.md:7, slide 1) states as a property that the system 'escalate[s] only untrustworthy cases to a human'. The project's own E2 experiment found the opposite on clean data: every clean-data escalation comes from the width rule and the escalated engines have the same or lower error rate than the acted-upon ones, so the escalated cases are not demonstrably the untrustworthy ones. The claim is supported only for injected faults (E3). The claim-evidence matrix even lists 'that abstention removes errors' under 'Claims deliberately NOT made', yet the headline implies exactly that selectivity.
verified.evidence: make_round1_slide.py:63 renders 'escalate only untrustworthy cases to a human'; README.md:3 'escalates only untrustworthy cases to a human'. experiments/results/e2_abstention/summary.json (loaded): FD001 error_rate_acted_upon 0.175 vs error_rate_among_escalated 0.143, relative_reduction -0.019; FD003 0.071 vs 0.071; conclusion 'NOT SUPPORTED' on 0/4; reasons are all 'insufficient_evidence'. docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:40 'width-based abstention does not concentrate wrong decisions'. CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md:30 'Claims deliberately NOT made: ... that abstention removes errors'.
verified.recommendation: Reword the thesis on the slide, README and deck slide 1 to what was measured, e.g. 'escalates corrupted, drifted or over-wide-interval cases to a human (input-trust escalation measured in E3; width escalation alone did not reduce decision errors, E2)'. Keep the word 'only' out unless E2 is re-run with a rule that does concentrate errors.

verdicts.reasoning: Every citation in the finding is literally present: submission/make_round1_slide.py:63, README.md:3 and submission/round2_deck_content.md:7 all say "escalate(s) only untrustworthy cases to a human", the rendered submission/round1_slide.png shows that text in the title band, and experiments/results/e2_abstention/summary.json contains exactly the quoted numbers (FD001 acted 0.175 vs escalated 0.143, rel -0.0185; FD003 0.071/0.071; 0/4 subsets; "NOT SUPPORTED"; reasons all insufficient_evidence). What does not hold up is the finding's central claim that the headline is "contradicted" by E2 and that this is high severity. (1) The project defines "untrustworthy" as a property of the evidence, not of the outcome: src/sentinelloop/agent.py lines 4-5 say "Escalation to a human happens when the evidence is not trustworthy: interval too wide, input quality bad, drift active while a serious order is due, or conflicting signals", and escalate = bool(reasons) (line 102). So "escalate only untrustworthy cases" is a true statement about the rule set (the agent escalates when and only when one of those four flags fires), and the Round 1 slide prints that rule table (ESCALATE row: interval wider than calibrated limit, >10% imputed inputs, drift active on HIGH/CRITICAL, anomaly vs RUL conflict) directly under the thesis. (2) E2 tested a different hypothesis, H2, "error rate among acted-upon engines is >=20% lower" (error concentration). The headline does not assert that, and CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md explicitly lists "that abstention removes errors" under claims deliberately NOT made, so the project is not making the claim the reviewer says E2 refutes. (3) The E2 negative result is already disclosed in the same documents: README.md:16 ("width-based abstention alone did not reduce decision errors (E2)") sits 13 lines below the thesis; deck slide 7 says "E2: width-based abstention does not concentrate errors (H2 rejected)"; matrix C11 and docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md carry it too. (4) The finding is filed under the prior_art dimension but has nothing to do with prior art. What survives is a low-priority wording polish: a lay judge may read "untrustworthy" as "would have produced a wrong order", which E2 shows is not true of width escalations on clean data; the slide content plan (submission/round1_slide_content.md, title band) originally used "escalates only exceptions to a human", which is the safer wording, and the deck slide 1 could say "cases whose inputs or evidence it cannot trust". Dropping "only", as the recommendation suggests, is not warranted: "only" is literally true of the code path. No judge is likely to penalise this given the rule table on the slide and the self-reported E2 negative result on the README and deck.

The project never uses it that way: src/sentinelloop/agent.py:4 defines escalation as "when the evidence is not trustworthy: interval too wide, input quality bad, drift active while a serious order is due, or conflicting signals", and docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md:6 says "send a human to inspect because the evidence is not trustworthy". verified.title: Lock file contains an editable install of this laptop's OneDrive path; README setup fails on any fresh machine
verified.issue: Line 76-77 read `# Editable install with no version control (sentinelloop==0.1.0)` / `-e c:\users\hp\onedrive\desktop\tata`. The lock is a verbatim `pip freeze` (diff against the venv's current `pip freeze` is empty). README line 22, DEMO_RUNBOOK line 8 and Makefile line 14 all run `pip install -r requirements.lock.txt`; pip parses the -e line first and aborts the entire install when the path does not exist, so no dependency is installed and step 3 (`pip install -e . --no-deps`) then yields a package with no numpy/pandas. On Linux/macOS the string is not even a path. DEMO_SCRIPT.md line 30 claims 'Everything you saw is reproducible from a clean clone with the commands in the README'. It also leaks the user name and folder.
verified.evidence: `pip install --dry-run --no-deps -e c:\users\nobody\desktop\tata` -> `ERROR: c:\users\nobody\desktop\tata is not a valid editable requirement. It should either be a path to a local project or a VCS URL`, exit 1. `diff <(sort requirements.lock.txt) <(sort pip-freeze)` -> no differences.
verified.recommendation: Regenerate with `pip list --format=freeze --exclude-editable > requirements.lock.txt` (or `pip freeze --exclude-editable`), delete lines 76-77, keep the explicit `pip install -e . --no-deps` step, and rehearse the README on a machine that is not this laptop before submission.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is literally true and in one respect understated. requirements.lock.txt lines 76-77 are exactly `# Editable install with no version control (sentinelloop==0.1.0)` / `-e c:\users\hp\onedrive\desktop\tata`; the file is byte-for-byte the venv's `pip freeze` (sorted diff empty), and README line 22, docs/DEMO_RUNBOOK.md line 8 and Makefile line 14 all run `pip install -r requirements.lock.txt` before `pip install -e . --no-deps`. The reviewer's dry-run reproduces (exit 1, same ERROR text). Worse than stated: pip's requirements-file parser (pip 26.2.1, `req_file.py`) passes option lines through `shlex.split`, which treats backslashes as escapes, so line 77 is read as `c:usershponedrivedesktoptata` and `pip install --dry-run --no-deps -r requirements.lock.txt` fails with exit 1 even on this laptop where the path exists, printing no 'Would install' line, i.e. nothing is installed on any platform. The error is not disclosed anywhere; the opposite is claimed: docs/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md item 18 calls the lock 'the reproducibility contract', docs/SCORING_AND_RISKS.md K3 marks it 'VERIFIED' and 'controlled', docs/THREAT_MODEL_AND_FAILURE_MODES.md C1 lists 'Fresh-clone run before submission' with no record it happened, and docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md line 30 claims clean-clone reproducibility. No Dockerfile exists despite K5 citing one. A judge following the README hits a hard error on the second command under a 20%-weighted 'working pipeline from a clean clone' criterion, so it would be penalised. I lower critical to high because the error message is self-explanatory, the fix is deleting two lines (or `pip install -e .` without `--no-deps`, since pyproject.toml declares all runtime dependencies with version ranges), the round-2 deck content does not itself cite the lock file, and no experimental result is invalidated; the damage is a failed first command plus a false 'VERIFIED' claim, not a broken pipeline.

verified.title: Lock pins pywin32==312 (Windows-only wheels) while README promises Windows, macOS or Linux
verified.issue: `pywin32==312` has no non-Windows distribution, so `pip install -r requirements.lock.txt` on macOS/Linux fails with 'No matching distribution found' (expected from pywin32's wheel set; not executed here). README line 18 header: 'Setup (Windows, macOS or Linux; Python 3.11+)'; line 22 says 'use .venv/bin/python elsewhere'. pywin32 is a transitive Windows-only dependency (docker/mlflow), not needed by the project.
verified.evidence: requirements.lock.txt line 69 `pywin32==312`; README.md line 18 `## Setup (Windows, macOS or Linux; Python 3.11+)`.
verified.recommendation: Use an environment marker (`pywin32==312; sys_platform == "win32"`) or generate the lock with pip-tools/uv so platform-specific pins carry markers; otherwise drop the macOS/Linux claim from the README.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding reproduces literally. requirements.lock.txt line 69 is `pywin32==312` with no environment marker; README.md line 18 is `## Setup (Windows, macOS or Linux; Python 3.11+)` and line 22 says `(use .venv/bin/python elsewhere)`. PyPI's file list for pywin32 312 contains 21 files, all `bdist_wheel` tagged win32/win_amd64/win_arm64 and no sdist, so a resolver on macOS/Linux cannot satisfy the pin and `pip install -r requirements.lock.txt` aborts with 'No matching distribution found'. pywin32 is purely transitive: `pip show pywin32` gives Required-by: docker; docker is required by mlflow; docker's own metadata declares it as `pywin32>=304; sys_platform == 'win32'`, i.e. the marker existed upstream and was flattened away by `pip freeze`. pyproject.toml does not list pywin32 and a grep of src/, docs/, configs, tests (excluding .venv) finds no win32 reference outside the lock line. Nothing discloses the lock as Windows-only; on the contrary docs/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md item 18 calls the lock file 'the reproducibility contract', docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md points to it for exact versions, and docs/SCORING_AND_RISKS.md ties the 20% 'Working pipeline' score to 'from a clean clone; lock file'. A judge on macOS/Linux following the README stops at step 2 with an error naming pywin32. Severity stays high because the project itself elevates this file to its reproducibility guarantee and advertises three platforms without qualification; the fix is a one-line marker or regenerating with pip-tools/uv. Aggravating adjacent defect the reviewer did not cite: line 77 `-e c:\users\hp\onedrive\desktop\tata` is a machine-specific absolute editable path, so the same lock also fails on any other Windows machine; after the pywin32 marker is added, that line still has to go (README line 23 already does `pip install -e . --no-deps` separately), or the lock remains non-installable on every clean clone.

verdicts.reasoning: Core of the finding reproduces: docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md line 63 says run_all.py "reproduces stages 1-6 in one command (expect 60-90 minutes...)", README line 38 and OFFICIAL_REQUIREMENTS R11 (line 60, "VERIFIED: one command, 33–46 s per subset, no manual step") repeat it, and no log under experiments/results/ shows a full-mode, all-subset run_all.py reaching its "ALL DONE" line. experiments/results/full_run.log has exactly run_all.py's sh() format ("$ cmd" / "-> exit 0 in 33 s"), completes FD001, starts FD002 at the "training point model" line and ends with a bare "exit=1" with no traceback; the stage-1 log shows FD002 finishing normally a minute later, so the exit=1 is an aborted/killed run, not a pipeline bug, but it is unexplained anywhere in the docs. All eight summary.json "generated" stamps match the finding exactly (e3 03:25:50, e1 03:29:23, e2 03:29:30, e6 03:31:27, e4 03:36:10, e7 03:38:42, e4_secondary 03:48:58, e5 04:04:02); artifacts/FD00x/metrics.json mtimes are 03:28:10/03:29:12/03:30:05/03:31:22 and oof/FD001_full_bl.csv 03:33:48, FD002_full_bl.csv 03:46:25, so E1/E2/E5 did run concurrently with the stage-5/6 scripts and "stage 4" (E5) finished after stage 6. run_all.py's order (pipeline, e1, e2, e5, e3, e4, e4sec, e6, e7) is confirmed from source. The "60-90 minutes" is an estimate, not a measurement. However the finding overstates in three ways, which lowers severity from high to medium: (1) the headline "the only recorded run_all.py invocation failed" is false — smoke_fast_fd001.log, _v2 and _v3 are run_all.py --fast --subsets FD001 runs that end with "ALL DONE in 3.5/1.3/2.2 min" and exit=0, so the script is demonstrated to run end to end, just not in full mode on all subsets; (2) staged execution is already disclosed (REPRODUCIBILITY line 52 table listing per-stage logs; EXPERIMENT_RESULTS line 3 "run in stages; logs full_run_stage*.log") and every stage log ends with exit=0 using the same scripts and flags run_all.py would issue; (3) the undisclosed concurrency is harmless for the numbers: only e3 and e4 read artifacts/ and both ran after the pipeline runs they depend on (e3 03:25:50 after stage 1 ended 03:23; e4 03:36:10 after the re-run ended 03:31:22), e1/e2/e5 use only the data and OOF caches, and the two pipeline runs are documented as giving identical metrics. What remains is a documentation overclaim a reliability judge would still note: "VERIFIED: one command" in R11 is only verified for the `run --subset all` half and for --fast FD001, the full wall time was never measured, and an abandoned exit=1 run_all.py log sits in results/ with no explanation.

verdicts.reasoning: The facts are accurate: full_run.log is the only run_all.py-format log, it ends at FD002 with exit=1, and nothing shows run_all.py completing. But 'high' is inflated for five reasons. (1) Nothing a judge is asked to trust depends on run_all.py. Every number in EXPERIMENT_RESULTS comes from summary.json files whose per-stage logs exist and end exit=0; the pipeline was run twice (stage 1 and stage 5) with identical metrics. (2) The official-requirement and deck claims rest on a different command. R11's 'VERIFIED: one command, 33-46 s per subset' is the pipeline `python -m sentinelloop run --subset all` (stage1 log, exit=0); CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C18 cites that same command and log; the Round 1 slide and Round 2 deck 'one command' lines refer to `sentinelloop run`. README line 38 merely describes what run_all.py does. Only REPRODUCIBILITY line 63 makes the untested 'reproduces stages 1-6 (60-90 min)' assertion. (3) The staged execution is already disclosed twice (REPRODUCIBILITY line 52 'executed in stages so that each stage stayed under 30 minutes; every stage log is kept'; EXPERIMENT_RESULTS line 3 'run in stages; logs full_run_stage*.log'), so a reader is not misled about provenance. (4) The abort is not evidence that run_all.py is broken. run_all.py's sh() logs '-> exit N' and raises SystemExit('step failed') on any child failure; neither line appears, nor any traceback, although stderr was captured (mlflow INFO/WARNING lines are present). The log mtime is 03:20:31, the FD002 model was never registered (stage 1 registers 'sentinelloop-FD002' version 1), and stage 1 began at 03:21:04: the process tree was killed within seconds of FD002 starting, consistent with the harness time limit that line 52 alludes to, not with a code failure. Every argument run_all.py passes matches the scripts' argparse (e1/e2/e5/e7 --subsets --fast; e3 --subsets only, and run_all correctly omits --fast; e4 --val-rows/--label-corruption/--out; e6 none; cli run --subset/--fast with stream-units default 5), and each of those commands exited 0 individually, so the composition has no identified failure point. (5) The 60-90 min figure matches the evidence: summing the logged stage wall times (stage1 ~2.5 min, E1 3.4, E2 <1, E5 33.6, E3 2.5, E4 4.5, E7 2.5, E4-secondary 8, E6 <1) gives ~60 min, and E5's timings were inflated by concurrent stages. The concurrency the finding notes is real (E5 ran 03:30-04:04 overlapping stages 5/6 and the tests; stage 2 overlapped the stage-5 pipeline rewrite while e1 reads artifacts/<subset>/predictions_test_all_cycles.csv), but the pipeline is deterministic with identical outputs on both runs and a torn read would crash rather than silently corrupt, so no number is affected. What survives is documentation hygiene: an unexplained exit=1 log sitting in the evidence folder, a wall-time estimate presented as an expectation without saying it is unmeasured, and a stage table whose numbering does not match the chronology. KNOWN_LIMITATIONS and FAILURE_ANALYSIS say nothing about this, so the recommendation (run it once from clean, or soften line 63 and explain/remove full_run.log) does add something, but a judge reading the deck would not penalise it and a judge running the code has no identified reason to hit a failure. Low, not high.

No code writes `e0_baseline` or the `FD00x_metrics.json` / `FD00x_predictions_test.csv` naming pattern (only submission/make_round1_slide.py reads it), and experiments/run_all.py never invokes the baseline, so the shipped E0 evidence has no producing code path: the files are baseline outputs (their key set is exactly baseline.py's `m` dict) copied and renamed by hand, and run.log is the cmd_baseline print output plus "exit=0". Compounding this, the E0 files carry config_hash 32521ec5.../49ee491d.../cfb02d8f.../9570cc56... while the current configs hash to 83fdcf31.../fd253a16.../f8eed413.../e32edc97... (configs/default.yaml was modified at 03:14, after the E0 run at 02:57-03:05), so a judge re-running the documented command cannot match the shipped files by hash and nothing explains why. The name collision is also real: pipeline.py:82-83 uses the same `Path(out_dir)/subset`, and pipeline.py:236-246 writes the same five names (metrics.json, predictions_test.csv, feature_manifest.json, clean_state.pkl, model_point.pkl). Running `baseline` after `run` replaces the pipeline's metrics.json (which has picp_test_capped, mpiw_test, escalation_share_test, conformal_qhat, agent_thresholds, mlflow_run_id, audit_chain_valid) with the baseline dict that lacks all of them, and replaces predictions_test.csv with a different schema (pred_hgbr/pred_rf/pred_naive instead of point/lower/upper/anomaly_score). No doc discloses this (grep for overwrite/clobber in docs, README, PROJECT_STATUS, submission: nothing relevant). However the finding overstates two consequences, which is why I lower the severity from high to medium. (1) The pickle/e3_stress consequence is benign in the default case: pipeline.py:90 calls baseline.prepare_frames(ds, cfg) and trains hgbr_all with the same train_point_model(seed, **mcfg), so clean_state.pkl, feature_manifest.json and model_point.pkl are content-identical (verified: dropped_sensors and n_features equal, hgbr RMSE identical to 2 dp on all four subsets); e3_stress.load_artifacts additionally reads model_cqr.pkl, anomaly.pkl, drift_monitor.pkl and agent_thresholds.json which baseline never touches. Only `baseline --fast` or `--seed N` would produce a divergent state/model. (2) The dashboard does not break: dashboard.py:54-58 and :101-102 use m.get(..., nan), so PICP/MPIW/escalation show as NaN/null rather than crashing, and viewdata.py:53 reads predictions_test_all_cycles.csv, not predictions_test.csv, so the Fleet/Engine views survive. Also mitigating: the C1 headline numbers are independently produced by the pipeline (artifacts/FD00x/metrics.json hgbr_rmse_capped 14.39/14.88/13.88/15.36 equals the E0 files), and REPRODUCIBILITY.md:43-44 lists the commands in the safe order (baseline then run). What remains is a genuine reproducibility defect a reliability judge would penalise: the documented command does not produce the cited folder, the C2 (RF/naive) and C3 (leaky-vs-honest CV) evidence exists only in hand-renamed files with a stale config hash, and re-running the E0 command silently degrades the pipeline's metrics.json without warning.

verified.issue: Step 3.2 runs `python -m sentinelloop run --subset FD001 --fast --stream-units 3` with the default `--out-dir artifacts`. pipeline.run writes to artifacts/FD001 (pipeline.py lines 82-84, 191, 221-249), unlinks and recreates artifacts/audit/decisions_FD001.jsonl (lines 172-175) and registers the fast model with `alias="champion"` (line 160). The pre-demo check on line 50 ('artifacts/ from a full (not fast) run present') is violated by the runbook's own step 2. verified.title: "Zero false alarms" is zero by construction, and the redefinition that made it so is undisclosed
verified.issue: README ("catch missing values, noise and regime shifts on 98–100% of corrupted engines with zero false alarms"), deck slide 8 ("0 false alarms"), DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 5 ("with zero false alarms") and EXPERIMENT_RESULTS E3 present 0.0 false alarms as a measured result. In experiments/e3_stress.py the false-alarm rate is `newly(u, full, base_full)` over clean engines, where `newly` is change-relative to a clean run of the same engines; `process()` recomputes everything from fixed training-fit artefacts per unit, so a clean engine's quality flag, anomaly flag and decision cannot change. The one fleet-level input that does change (the drift alarm, passed to `decide(..., drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm)`) adds the `drift_active` escalation (agent.py:98), but `newly` only checks ("data_quality", "conflicting_evidence"), contrary to its own docstring which lists "drift". So clean HIGH/CRITICAL engines newly escalated for drift are not counted as false alarms. DECISION_LOG D19 records that the change-relative definition was adopted after the absolute definition gave 52% false alarms (FAILURE_ANALYSIS §1 row 5). No submission document says the metric is change-relative or that the absolute rate was 52%.
verified.evidence: e3_stress.py:5-10 docstring: "Everything is CHANGE-RELATIVE to the clean run of the same engines... false alarm(u) = the same signals on CLEAN engines (which, being unchanged, can only come from the quality monitor or a fleet-level drift alarm)"; e3_stress.py:120 `esc_new = any(... for r in ("data_quality", "conflicting_evidence"))`; agent.py:97-98 `if obs.drift_flag and severity in ("HIGH","CRITICAL"): reasons.append("drift_active")`; summary.json: `fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail` is true in all 20 rows; DECISION_LOG D19: "counting them as false alarms (52%) was wrong".
verified.recommendation: State in README, deck slide 8 and demo script that detection and false alarms are change-relative to a clean run and that the absolute false-alarm rate on clean late-life engines was 52%; either include `drift_active` in `newly()` and re-report, or report separately the share of clean engines escalated for drift in each scenario. Drop the phrase "zero false alarms" unless that number survives.

verdicts.reasoning: Partly reproduced, partly refuted. CONFIRMED: experiments/e3_stress.py:121 `newly()` tests only ("data_quality","conflicting_evidence") while the docstring (lines 7-8) and the generated experiments/results/e3_stress/README.md both publish the definition as "newly raised escalation (data_quality / conflicting_evidence / drift)". src/sentinelloop/agent.py:97-98 adds `drift_active` for HIGH/CRITICAL when drift_flag is set; in E3 `full` uses drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm (True in all 20 summary.json rows) and `base_full` uses False, so every clean HIGH/CRITICAL engine gets a new drift_active escalation that the metric ignores. Reproducing the seed-42 clean split against artifacts/FD00x/decisions_test.csv, that is 12/50, 34/130, 14/50 and 25/124 clean engines (20-28%) per scenario; under the published definition the false-alarm rate would be ~0.2-0.28 on every row and H3's <=0.05 criterion would fail, so the headline "zero false alarms" (README:16, deck slide 8, DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 5, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS E3) rests on a narrower definition than the one the evidence artefact states. REFUTED parts: (1) "zero by construction" is overstated: the window quality flag term `uq1[u]["flag"]` is absolute (pipeline.window_quality is per-unit against the fixed training reference, clean.impute is per-unit), and EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md line 51 itself says this term produced 18% false alarms before D20, so the 0.0 is a genuinely measured quality-monitor false-positive rate, not a tautology; only the anomaly and data_quality/conflicting_evidence terms are zero by construction. (2) "No submission document says the metric is change-relative or that the absolute rate was 52%" is false: EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:41 ("signals change-relative to the clean run"), the E3 results README, PROJECT_STATUS.md:37, DECISION_LOG D19 (with the 52%) and FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md section 1 row 5 (52% "false alarms", with the reason) all state it, and README:5 names docs/ as the evidence location. The change-relative definition is also methodologically sound for a fault-injection test (end-of-life anomalies on clean engines are true anomaly-detector positives, not stress-test false alarms), so a judge would not penalise the redefinition itself or demand the 52% in the README. What survives is a definition/code mismatch that materially favours the headline number and is not surfaced in README, deck or demo script (the code comment at lines 111-112 says the fleet alarm is "reported separately", which the table does via fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail, but nothing says 20-28% of clean engines are escalated to a human in every scenario). That is a real "misleading" item but, given the disclosures already present and the arguable correctness of escalating during a genuine fleet-wide corruption, medium rather than high.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding's central claim, that the 0.0 false-alarm rate is zero by construction, misreads e3_stress.py:122. `newly()` returns `uq1[u]["flag"] or a_new or esc_new`; the quality-flag term is ABSOLUTE, not change-relative. `pipeline.window_quality` is per-unit and `DriftMonitor.quality` compares each engine's trailing window to fixed `ref_min/ref_max` from the pickled monitor, so for clean engines `false_alarm_rate` equals the share of the 354 clean late-life test engines the quality monitor flags. That number can be non-zero (it was 18% in the fast diagnostic before D20, FAILURE_ANALYSIS §1 row 3) and the main clean run independently confirms 0 `data_quality` escalations at the last cycle on all 507 test engines across the four subsets. So "zero false alarms" is a genuine measurement of the per-engine input-quality monitor, which is what the headline claim is about. The parts that ARE zero by construction (new anomaly flag, new data_quality/conflicting_evidence escalation on an unchanged engine) are exactly what D19 intended to exclude: a health-index anomaly on a clean engine near failure is a degradation true positive, so the 52% "absolute" figure was the anomaly detector working, not a false-alarm rate. The recommendation to print "absolute false-alarm rate was 52%" in the deck would make the deck less accurate, not more. The "undisclosed" claim is also wrong for the evidence documents: docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md:41 (the document README line 16 explicitly cites for details) says "signals change-relative to the clean run", experiments/results/e3_stress/README.md says the same, PROJECT_STATUS.md:37 names "D19/D20 change-relative stress metrics", and docs/FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md §1 row 5 plus DECISION_LOG D19 give the 52% number with its root cause. No absolute definition was pre-registered (EXPERIMENT_PLAN E3 lists measured signals only; H3 says "false-alarm rate ≤ 5% on clean windows" without a definition), and D19 was fixed on the fast diagnostic before the full four-subset run, the same way D20 was. A judge reading the deck would not be misled about anything a careful reader of the cited results doc could not find, and an ML reviewer who checks the code finds a real quality-monitor measurement, not a tautology. What survives is low-severity polish: (1) the docstring (lines 7-8) and the E3 results README list "drift" in the detection definition while the code deliberately excludes it (code comment lines 111-112, verdict text "Fleet-level drift alarms are reported separately"); (2) the share of clean HIGH/CRITICAL engines (22-29% per subset from decisions_test.csv) routed to INSPECTION via `drift_active` in every scenario is not reported, although the fleet alarm is a correct true positive (half the fleet is corrupted) and the escalation is the safe direction; (3) the headline sentences in README, deck slide 8, DEMO_SCRIPT and C12 could carry a "change-relative to a clean run" qualifier. None of these would cost points with a competition judge; severity "high" for the misleading dimension is inflated.

verified.title: "Silent-wrong-order rate driven to zero" is produced by the fleet drift alarm escalating every HIGH/CRITICAL engine, not by per-engine detection
verified.issue: Deck slide 8 ("silent-wrong-order rate 0 (full agent) vs 2–19% (point-threshold agent)"), README line 16 and DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 5 ("went from 2–19% to zero") present this as the quality monitors catching bad inputs. In E3 the full agent receives `drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm`, which was True in all 20 scenarios, and agent.py escalates every HIGH/CRITICAL decision when drift is active; `silent_wrong` counts only non-escalated HIGH/CRITICAL orders, so it is structurally 0 for the full agent whenever the fleet alarm fires. The naive agent is run with `drift_alarm=False`. The bias rows make this visible: per-engine detection is 4–20% on FD001/FD003 yet silent-wrong-order is still 0. Also, the naive rate is 0.000 in 3 of 20 rows (FD001 regime_shift, FD003 missing20, FD003 regime_shift), so "2–19% → zero" overstates the baseline, and denominators are 50 engines on FD001/FD003 (0.04 = 2 engines).
verified.evidence: e3_stress.py:116-117 `full = decide(last1, uq1, thr, drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm, use_quality=True)` / `naive = decide(..., drift_alarm=False, use_quality=False)`; e3_stress.py:131 `silent_wrong` requires `not decs[u].escalate_to_human`; summary.json: all 20 `fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail` true; FD001 bias2s detection_rate 0.12, silent_wrong_order_full 0.0; rows with silent_wrong_order_naive == 0: FD001 regime_shift, FD003 missing20, FD003 regime_shift.
verified.recommendation: Say explicitly that the full agent's zero comes mostly from the fleet-level drift rule (escalate all HIGH/CRITICAL while a fleet alarm is active) and report the cost of that rule (share of clean HIGH/CRITICAL engines escalated). Replace "2–19%" with "0–19%" and give engine counts alongside rates.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding reproduces literally. (1) experiments/e3_stress.py lines 116-117 build the full agent with drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm and the naive agent with drift_alarm=False, use_quality=False; line 71 applies that single fleet-level boolean to every unit. (2) src/sentinelloop/agent.py triage(): `if obs.drift_flag and severity in ("HIGH","CRITICAL"): reasons.append("drift_active")`, then `escalate = bool(reasons)`, so every HIGH/CRITICAL decision is escalated while the alarm is on. (3) e3_stress.py line 130 counts silent_wrong only when `not decs[u].escalate_to_human`. Together these make silent_wrong_order_full an identity 0 for any row where the fleet alarm fired. (4) experiments/results/e3_stress/summary.json: fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail is True in all 20 rows, so the zero is structural in every row, not an empirical detection outcome; the H3 criterion "silent-wrong-order reduced >= 50%" is therefore trivially met for every fault, including the two bias faults whose per-engine detection is 0.04-0.20 (FD001 bias2s detection 0.12, silent_wrong_order_full 0.0; escalation reasons show drift_active 16 vs no data_quality at all). (5) silent_wrong_order_naive == 0.0 in exactly 3 of 20 rows (FD001 regime_shift, FD003 missing20, FD003 regime_shift), so "2-19%" should be "0-19%"; n_corrupted is 50 on FD001/FD003, so 0.04 is 2 engines. (6) The baseline comparison is not like-for-like: the naive agent has the drift rule hard-disabled, and the false_alarm_rate (newly() at lines 119-122) deliberately excludes drift_active, so the cost of the blanket rule on clean HIGH/CRITICAL engines is never reported. Disclosure check: docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md line 51 and the E3 README state that the fleet alarm fired in every scenario and list drift_active counts, but no document says the zero follows mechanically from the escalate-all-HIGH/CRITICAL rule; EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md phrases it as "The full agent never issued a confident wrong order", and the deck (slide 8), README line 16, DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 5 and CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C12 (marked VERIFIED) all present it as a headline stress-test result. Given the project's explicit honest-evidence framing and that this is a repeated headline number, a judge who notices that detection is 4-20% yet silent-wrong is 0 would reasonably treat the claim as misleading. Severity high is warranted; the recommended fix (state the mechanism, report the clean-engine escalation cost, write 0-19% with engine counts) is accurate.

verdicts.reasoning:
The mechanism is literally true and I confirmed it: src/sentinelloop/agent.py:97-98 escalates every HIGH/CRITICAL decision when drift_flag is set; experiments/e3_stress.py:116 passes drift_alarm=rep_fleet_tail.alarm to the full agent and :117 passes False to the naive one; :131 silent_wrong requires not escalate_to_human; summary.json shows fleet_drift_alarm_mixed_tail=True in all 20 rows. So silent_wrong_order_full=0 is guaranteed by construction in every row. The 'reasons' block in summary.json sharpens this: on FD001 bias2s/bias3s there are 0 data_quality escalations (only drift_active 16/15 and insufficient_evidence 7), so without the drift input the full agent would have exactly the naive rate (0.04); FD003 bias rows have 1 data_quality escalation vs 2-3 silent-wrong engines. The three naive=0.000 rows (FD001 regime_shift, FD003 missing20, FD003 regime_shift) and the 50-engine denominators also check out.

Why it is not 'high': (1) the drift-escalation rule is the real deployed behaviour, not an experiment shortcut (pipeline.py:180 and :216 feed drift_report.alarm into every observation), and the pre-registered H3 hypothesis and E3 plan explicitly name 'quality monitor AND drift detector' vs 'agent without quality/drift inputs' as the comparison; (2) the ingredients are disclosed: deck slide 6, round1 slide and DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 6 list 'drift active on HIGH/CRITICAL' as an escalation rule, and the EXPERIMENT_RESULTS E3 table has a 'fleet drift alarm: yes (all)' column beside the silent-wrong-order column, with drift_active counts in summary.json; (3) for 10 of 20 rows (missing20 x4, regime_shift x4, noise3s on FD002/FD004) data_quality escalations cover 100% of corrupted engines, so the zero would hold without the drift rule; the finding's blanket 'not by per-engine detection' overstates the dependence. Most competition judges scoring Agent behaviour/Demo would not trace this.

Why it is not refuted: nothing states that the zero follows by construction once the fleet alarm fires, KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md and FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md are silent on it, the cost of the rule on clean HIGH/CRITICAL engines is not reported anywhere (false_alarm_rate deliberately excludes drift escalations via newly(), so the deck's '0 false alarms' sits next to an uncounted conversion of clean serious orders to INSPECTION), and the headline sentences (README line 16 'drive the silent-wrong-order rate to zero', deck slide 8, DEMO_SCRIPT Beat 5 '2-19% to zero', CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C12, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS 'never issued a confident wrong order') read as a per-engine monitoring achievement. DECISION_LOG D11 names this metric as one of four differentiators, and the deck's positioning is 'honest evidence', so an ML reviewer who notices '0 in 20/20 rows beside 4% detection' would downgrade a core claim. The '2-19%' range also contradicts the project's own table (three 0.00 cells), including inside EXPERIMENT_RESULTS prose. The recommendation (one sentence attributing the zero to the fleet-drift rule, one number for clean serious orders escalated, '0-19%' with engine counts) is concrete and cheap. Net: medium.

verified.title: FD004 champion (PICP 0.82) fails the system's own promotion-gate floor and was never gated
verified.issue: The slide's side loop advertises "promotion gate (RMSE, coverage ≥ 0.85, late-order rate)" next to FD004 results, the README thesis says the system "retrains only through a promotion gate", and deck slide 9 repeats "PICP ≥ 0.85". The pipeline registers the initial model as `champion` unconditionally (no gate), and the FD004 champion's test coverage is 0.8226, below the 0.85 floor the gate would apply to any challenger. FAILURE_ANALYSIS §2.4 admits "the PICP gate threshold (0.85) would have flagged FD004" but README, slide and deck do not.
verified.evidence: src/sentinelloop/pipeline.py:160 `model_name=f"sentinelloop-{subset}", alias="champion"` with no `evaluate_gate` call (grep of pipeline.py/cli.py for "retrain|evaluate_gate" returns nothing); artifacts/FD004/metrics.json `picp_test_capped` 0.8225806; FAILURE_ANALYSIS line 22.
verified.recommendation: State on slide 5 / README that the initial champion is registered without the gate and that FD004's champion would not pass the gate's coverage floor as shipped; or gate the initial registration and report the outcome.

verdicts.reasoning: The raw facts reproduce, but the finding's central claim does not, and it misquotes the cited slide. (1) Misquote: submission/round1_slide_content.md line 12 reads "promotion gate (RMSE, coverage, late-order rate)" with no "≥ 0.85"; grep for "0.85" or "≥" in that file returns nothing. The 0.85 floor appears only in deck slide 9, configs/default.yaml and KNOWN_LIMITATIONS 10. (2) Wrong metric: the gate never scores the official test set. experiments/e4_retrain_gate.py (docstring and validation_metrics()) and docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md line 54 state the gate's RMSE/PICP are computed on a 20% held-out validation split of training engines; the 0.8226 in artifacts/FD004/metrics.json is picp_test_capped on the official C-MAPSS test set, which is a reporting number the gate should never see. On the gate's own metric the FD004 champion scores champion_picp 0.94 (5 rows/engine) and 0.954 (20 rows/engine) in artifacts/FD004/retrain_log.json, well above 0.85. So "the FD004 champion would not pass the gate's coverage floor as shipped" is false; the project's own FAILURE_ANALYSIS line 22 sentence is loose in the same direction but errs against the project, not for it. (3) "Never gated" is inherent, not misleading: evaluate_gate(champion, challenger, cfg) compares a challenger against an existing champion (rmse_limit = champion rmse x 1.02, late_limit = champion late_rate + 0.02); the first model cannot be gated against itself. README line 3 and deck slide 1 say "retrains only through a gate", and retrains (E4 challengers) are the only path that goes through it; initial training is not a retrain. (4) Already disclosed: FD004 PICP 0.82 is printed in README table line 14, README line 16 ("FD004 coverage is below nominal: all reported, none hidden"), deck slide 5 ("FD004 under-coverage shown"), slide 10, CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C4, KNOWN_LIMITATIONS 5 and FAILURE_ANALYSIS 2.4; the absolute-floor weakness of the gate is disclosed in KNOWN_LIMITATIONS 21, deck slide 9 and slide 10. The 0.82 figure is official test-set coverage, which the gate cannot consume at promotion time without test-label leakage. (2) The under-coverage itself is disclosed everywhere a judge would look: README results table shows 0.82 under the "90% interval coverage" header and line 16 says "FD004 coverage is below nominal: all reported, none hidden"; deck slide 5 says "FD004 under-coverage shown, asymmetric CQR option (0.839 → 0.863)"; deck slide 9 and 10 state the absolute floor rejected better challengers and must be made relative; KNOWN_LIMITATIONS 5, 10, 21; CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX C4; DEMO_SCRIPT line 28; PROJECT_STATUS line 49. (3) The slide and README describe the gate as a RETRAINING gate ("retrains only through a gate"; slide line 34 "challenger → gate → promote or reject"). The gate is a champion-vs-challenger comparison (rmse ≤ champion+2%, late_rate ≤ champion+0.02) and has no champion to compare the bootstrap model against; registering the initial model ungated is standard practice and no ML reviewer would read the thesis as claiming otherwise. (4) The Round 1 slide (the cited file) does not display coverage at all, only RMSEs (line 37), so there is no on-slide juxtaposition of 0.82 with 0.85. The recommendation reduces to a one-phrase clarification ("initial model registered; subsequent challengers gated") that no judge would penalise the absence of; the second half of the recommendation would insert a claim that is technically wrong. "High" is inflated; at most a low-priority wording tweak.

Slide 7 does not retract it; it qualifies it with a defensible answer to 'why the lower bound' (lower late rate at 11/16 tuned frontier points, removes FD004's only late orders, 0 vs 0.006). (2) The trade-off is disclosed everywhere, including inside the deck itself: slide 2 explicitly promises 'negative results are on slides 7 and 9'; slide 7 says 'conservative operating point the operator chooses, not a free lunch'; docs/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md E1 finding 4 (line 24); docs/FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md section 2 item 1 and section 3 ('the interval is justified only when the operator values late-rate control above discarded life... stated to the operator, not assumed'); README line 16 ('conservative operating point, not a free improvement'); docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md line 19 ('we do not claim the interval policy is free'); submission/CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md C10 ('NOT SUPPORTED, negative result kept'). (3) The substantive part of the recommendation is already applied: README line 16 leads 'what the experiments showed' with E3, then E6, then E4-B2, and only then the E1/E2 negatives; docs/INNOVATION_HYPOTHESES.md line 10 already records that 'the differentiation claim is re-weighted toward H2, H3, H4 and H6; H1 is kept as the evaluation backbone'. (4) The recommended replacement wording would introduce an unsupported claim: '0 vs up to 19% for a point-threshold agent' mislabels the E3 comparator. The E3 naive agent is the same rule agent with quality/drift inputs switched off (experiments/e3_stress.py lines 93 and 117: use_quality=False, drift_alarm=False; e3_stress/README.md line 3), not a point-threshold agent; the 2-19% figure says nothing about point vs lower bound. (5) The rubric (Working pipeline 20, Data eng 15, Model perf 15, MLOps 10, Agent 10, Coverage 10, Demo & explanation 20) has no 'thesis leads with the strongest result' item; honest 'this is a tunable operating point' framing is as likely to read as rigour as as weakness to an ML reviewer. verified.title: 'Escalates only untrustworthy cases to a human' is contradicted by the entry's own audit logs and E2
verified.issue: The README, the rendered Round 1 slide title band and Round 2 slide 1 all say the agent 'escalates only untrustworthy cases'. On clean official test data every escalation is width-triggered (insufficient_evidence) plus a few conflicting_evidence; none is a data-quality or drift escalation (quality_flag_rate_test 0.0, drift_alarm_test false). E2 shows those escalated engines are no more error-prone than the acted-upon ones (FD001: 0.143 among escalated vs 0.175 acted-upon). So 7-15% of clean-data engines are sent to a human with no measured decision benefit; that is human workload without return, and the deck never states this cost in business terms (inspections per 100 machines).

On slide 6 add the clean-data cost explicitly (e.g. 'FD001: 15 inspections per 100 engines on clean data, no measured error reduction; the width rule earns its keep only on corrupted inputs, E3').
